questions.question: When should you use a fast-forward merge?
choices: When both branches have made changes to the same file
When the source branch's base is the tip of the target branch
When you want to preserve the exact timeline of commits
When there are many merge conflicts to resolve
questions.explanation: Fast-forward is possible when the source branch's first commit is the same as the target's latest commit — meaning no divergence occurred. This gives a clean, linear history.

questions.question: What causes a merge conflict?
choices: When the source branch has more commits than the target
When both branches modify the same file
When you try to merge a feature branch into main
When the target branch has no commits
questions.explanation: Conflicts arise when both branches have changes to the same file. Git cannot automatically determine which version to keep, so manual resolution is needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'up-to-date' and 'fast-forward'?
choices: They are the same thing with different names
Up-to-date means source has no new commits; fast-forward means source has new linear commits
Up-to-date is for main branch; fast-forward is for feature branches
Fast-forward requires a merge commit; up-to-date does not
questions.explanation: Up-to-date means source has zero commits ahead of target (nothing to merge). Fast-forward means source has new commits that are linear extensions of target's history.
